verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that ṣāfiāt denotes groups arranged in ranks, zājirāt those who ward off by warning, and tāliyāt those who recite. Exegetes variously identify them as angels, worshippers or fighters, Qur’anic prohibitions, angels governing clouds, or Qur’an reciters; tāliyāt in particular has been taken as angels reciting revelation or the decree, or reciters in prayer.

Possibly—and God knows best—the three are groups of angels descending with revelation, who line up along its path, drive off shayāṭīn so that revelation reaches its intended prophet uncorrupted, and recite the dhikr to him. This may specifically concern the Prophet Muḥammad, in light of the divine guards sent before and behind a chosen messenger (72:26–28). The dhikr may mean revelation generally or, more likely from tāliyāt, the Qur’an. The subsequent mention of shooting stars repelling shayāṭīn and the question of creation in (37:11) support this reading.

Their participation does not contradict the Qur’an’s attribution of the Qur’an’s descent to Jibrāʾīl: they are his aides, while he remains responsible for the task, just as angelic messengers take souls under the leadership of the Angel of Death. The feminine plural forms do not exclude angels, since malāʾikah is grammatically feminine when denoting a group. This chapter is the Qur’an’s first to open with oaths; God swears by created things because their created and sustained existence derives all their honor and splendor from Him.

verses.4: Al-Mizan states that “Surely, your Lord is One” addresses all humanity and is the assertion for which the preceding oaths are sworn; its arguments follow later.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan holds that “The Lord of the heavens and the earth” may be a second predicate of the preceding statement, the predicate of an implied subject, or an apposition to “One.” It indicates why God alone is the true deity: divinity worthy of worship belongs to the Lord who administers creation, and He manages the heavens, the earth, and all between them.

The angels’ descent with revelation illustrates this governance. They stand between heaven and earth, repel shayāṭīn from interfering, and recite revelation to the Prophet, thereby perfecting and nurturing humanity whether people accept it or not. Thus the management involved in revelation confirms that He is the one Lord of all.

“The Lord of the eastern horizons” may mean the seasonally varying points of sunrise, the eastern rising-places of all stars including the sun, or eastern horizons generally. Its mention suits revelation, which dawns from heaven through the angels.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains zīnah as ornament or adornment, with al-kawākib either explaining it or standing in apposition to it: the heavens are adorned with stars, as elsewhere described through lamps and lanterns. The samāʾ is evidently one of the seven heavens, the realm of stars above the earth, though some exegetes prefer readings conforming to ancient or modern cosmology.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes ḥifẓan as the object of an omitted cognate verb: God has protected the heavens with a protection from every rebellious shayṭān. A shayṭān is a malevolent, wicked, vicious jinn wholly devoid of goodness.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains lā yassammaʿūna as eavesdropping, a figurative expression for the shayāṭīn’s exclusion from the heavenly realm and their being driven away, not an inherent inability to hear; otherwise casting them out would be needless. The exalted assembly, al-malaʾ al-aʿlā, consists of the honored angels in the heights of heaven, whom the shayāṭīn seek to overhear.

Their eavesdropping means trying to obtain guarded news of the unseen relating to the earthly world, including future events. Yuqdhafūn means they are thrown, cast, or shot away, while jānib means every side.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains duḥūran as being repelled, expelled, or banished—grammatically, it may be a circumstantial verbal noun, a causative object, or the cognate object of an omitted verb. Wāṣib means permanent, lasting, or binding, so the shayāṭīn are driven off and face enduring torment.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains khaṭfah as snatching, here stealing an opportunity to listen; the exception applies to the subject of “they cannot listen,” although some exegetes allow an independent exception clause. Shihāb is a visible shooting star or meteor, and thāqib, “piercing,” signifies that it does not miss its target. Thus the lowest heaven is adorned with stars and guarded against every wicked shayṭān: they are barred from learning news of the unseen from the exalted assembly, cast away, banished, and assigned lasting punishment, except that one may seize a fragment before a piercing flame pursues it.

Exegetical depictions of celestial spheres surrounding the earth, with gated angelic realms and angels lying in wait with shooting stars to strike eavesdropping shayāṭīn, arose from the immediate sense of the verses and from traditions. Al-Mizan judges the scientific inaccuracy of such depictions clear and says that many—including views found in al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr by al-Rāzī and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī by al-Ālūsī—have consequently been abandoned.

Possibly—and God knows best—the descriptions are figurative portrayals of supernatural realities in forms graspable by the senses, as with Qur’anic analogies and such realities as the throne, divine seat, tablet, and Book. On this reading, “heaven” is the realm of malakūt inhabited by angels, having a higher horizon relative to the visible world. The shayāṭīn approach that realm to learn the secrets of creation and future events but are expelled because they cannot endure the light of the malakūt. Alternatively, they seize truth in order to combine it with deception, and the angels repel them with the truth that dispels their lies. This interpretation is supported by the passage’s placement after the oaths by the angels of revelation and the statement that they protect revelation from shayāṭīn.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains lāzib as firmly adhering or stuck together; Majmaʿ al-Bayān glosses it as lāzim, “necessary,” “binding,” or “affixed.” “The ones We created” may refer either to the angels who guard revelation and strike shayāṭīn with shooting stars, or to great creations besides human beings, such as the heavens, earth, and angels; the plural pronoun may encompass animate and inanimate beings.

The verse challenges people to compare their creation with those greater creations. Since they were made from sticky clay, they are among God’s least powerful creations and have no power over Him.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet marvels at people treating him as a liar while he calls them to the truth. Their mockery may be directed at his astonishment, at his call to the truth, or at their own refusal to heed reminders of God’s signs leading to divine oneness and the true religion.

verses.14: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains that sakhira and istaskhara both mean mocking. Thus, when the polytheists see a miraculous sign of God, they ridicule it.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that their calling God’s signs “this” displays their inability to regard them as significant; it is their strongest form of belittlement and mockery.
verses.16: Al-Mizan holds that they deny resurrection solely because restoring someone after death, when the body has become dust and bones, seems impossible to them. Their repeated rhetorical questions about both themselves and their ancient forefathers show that they are overwhelmed by the imagined impossibility of resurrection, especially for forefathers of whom only stories remain. Had their objection instead been that death entails utter nonexistence and thus prevents return, one question would have covered both themselves and their forefathers.

They call it yawm al-dīn rather than yawm al-baʿth because their realization concerns requital; its past-tense wording expresses the certainty of its occurrence. “The day of sorting,” yawm al-faṣl, is either spoken by people to one another or, more likely in light of the following verse, by angels or God. It is the day when divine judgment distinguishes truth from falsehood, or separates the guilty from the God-conscious.

verses.22:
Al-Mizan takes the command to gather the unjust as God’s address to the angels, though some hold that angels address one another. The unjust are not all who ever committed an injustice, but the polytheists whose defining worldly course was stubborn rejection and combat against the truth. Their azwājuhum most apparently means their associates among the shayāṭīn; readings of it as fellow sinners or disbelieving wives are weak, since they do not fit the description of the unjust in the verse.

What they worship besides Allah primarily means their false idols, though it may possibly include worshipped sentient beings such as Pharaohs and Nimrods; angels and Jesus are excluded. To lead them to jaḥīm means to deliver and cast them into hell. Majmaʿ al-Bayān describes this as guidance used in place of guidance to paradise, and hence as sarcastic.

In substance, they are questioned about the arrogance by which they refused all the truth in worldly life, including true beliefs and righteous deeds.

verses.27:
Al-Mizan describes a blaming quarrel at the resurrection between followers and those they followed. The followers accuse their leaders of having approached them “from the right,” that is, under the guise of good will and guidance; interpreting “right” as religion is similar, whereas interpreting it as power or might is doubtful.

Those followed deny that they deprived their followers of faith or possessed real authority over them. Any power they had was yielded to them by their followers, who were obligated to submit to the truth. The followers were unbelieving and ṭāghīn, a people who crossed the bounds; both groups arrogantly persisted in forsaking guidance. Thus the Lord’s sentence has come due against them, and they will taste the punishment.

verses.32: Al-Mizan presents this statement as part of the causal course ending in the decree of punishment: rebelliousness produces misguidance, and misguidance leads to hell. The leaders led their followers astray only after the followers freely embraced obstinate rebellion, attached themselves to the leaders, and allowed their misguidance to spread to them. They were not coerced or enslaved, so they merited the divine sentence.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains that both followers and leaders share punishment because both shared injustice and crime, so neither gains an advantage over the other. This does not require equal measures of punishment: each receives what suits his circumstances, and, as some exegetes argue, those who misled others may bear their own burdens as well as burdens connected with those they misled. The guilty are the polytheists, whose arrogance made them refuse divine unity and the word of sincerity when it was presented to them.

verses.36: Al-Mizan explains that, after arrogantly rejecting divine unity, they deny the message by asking whether they should abandon their gods for a mad poet. The reply refutes both the charge against the Prophet and their dismissal of God’s Book as poetry or deranged speech: he brought the truth and confirmed the preceding messengers. verses.38: Al-Mizan presents this as a threat of painful punishment for their arrogance and their attempt to oppose truth with falsehood.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that their requital is not unjust: their own deeds are returned to them.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan treats the exception for the purified servants of Allah as absolute, not inclusive. It may exclude them from those who taste severe punishment, or from those requited only according to their deeds, in which case their known sustenance is beyond such requital. Reading it as an inclusive exception is weak; moreover, taking it specifically as an exception to the implied pronoun in “you will only be requited for what you did” is problematic.

They are God’s servants, having no will or deeds apart from what God wills, and they are mukhlaṣūn rather than mukhliṣūn: God has purified them. They associate nothing with Him and are unattached to all else, whether worldly adornment or even blessings of the hereafter. Their “known sustenance” therefore denotes a distinct, chosen, heavenly sustenance exclusive to them, reflecting their lofty rank, even if others share basic food and drink. Interpretations that make it merely sustenance with known qualities, sustenance at a set time, or simply Paradise are weak.

verses.44: Al-Mizan explains that surur is the ordinary plural of sarīr, an elevated seat or throne. Facing one another signifies convivial familiarity and delight in looking at one another, rather than sitting turned away.
verses.45: Al-Mizan explains that a kaʾs is a drinking vessel containing a drink; an empty vessel is called a qadaḥ. Maʿīn suggests clear water flowing over the land, and here denotes the pure, exquisitely tasting drink subsequently described as white.
verses.46: Al-Mizan explains that the drink’s pure whiteness makes it delicious to those who drink it. Ladhdhah is either an intensified verbal noun or the feminine form of ladhdh, “delicious.”
verses.47: Al-Mizan explains that ghawl means harm or decay, while yunzafūn means being deprived of one’s intellect through drunkenness. The wine of paradise has none of the harms of worldly wine and does not intoxicate its drinkers into mindlessness.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains that the verse describes the heavenly ḥūr granted to the people of paradise. Qāṣirāt al-ṭarf, “maidens of modest gaze,” figuratively conveys coy, coquettish gazes, while ʿayn denotes large, beautiful eyes. Some exegetes instead take qāṣirāt al-ṭarf to mean that their gaze and love are confined to their husbands, and take ʿayn to refer to intensely black centers contrasting with the whites of the eyes.
verses.49: Al-Mizan glosses bayḍ maknūn (37:49): bayḍ is the collective noun “eggs,” with bayḍah its singular, and maknūn means “hidden” or “treasured away.” Some exegetes understand the comparison as eggs concealed by feathers in a nest or something similar, untouched and sheltered from dust; others as an egg’s interior before it is cracked open and anyone can lay hands on it.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that some of the sincere, purified servants in paradise speak to one another about people and events from worldly life. One recalls a particular human companion—not a personal shayṭān—who mocked belief in resurrection and judgment. Although Satan might possibly appear to such servants without influencing their hearts, their purified state prevents them from being swayed by a demonic companion.

The speaker asks others whether they wish to look down, then sees his former companion in the middle of hell. He swears that the companion almost brought about his destruction, as though causing him to fall into that hellpit, but says that his Lord’s niʿmah—blessing, grace, and guidance—saved him from being summoned for punishment with him.

His question about no death after the first death and no punishment is an exclamation of wonder and joyful certainty, not a genuine question. “The first death” is the ordinary death of worldly life; though another death exists in barzakh, it is disregarded because this is the death people had considered the absolute end. He extols eternal blessed life and deliverance from punishment as the great victory. Al-Mizan holds that “For this, then, let those who would strive, strive” most fittingly remains his speech: in the abode of responsibility, people should strive for this victory, though others attribute the words to God, angels, or the inhabitants of paradise.

verses.62:
Al-Mizan contrasts the noble welcome prepared for the people of paradise with the welcome of the people of the fire: the tree of Zaqqūm and boiling ḥamīm. Nuzul is what is prepared for an arriving guest. “Better” does not attribute any goodness to Zaqqūm, but contrasts it with the better provision that is with God.

Zaqqūm is made a fitnah—calamity and torment—for the unjust. It grows from the depths of hell; this should not be thought astonishing, since human beings themselves will subsist eternally in the fire, and God does what He wills. Its ṭalʿ, the first fruit or spathes of a tree, is likened to demons’ heads because people conventionally imagine demons in the ugliest forms. The comparison does not require listeners to have seen demons’ heads.

The unjust eat this tree as their welcoming repast, filling their bellies because extreme hunger drives them to consume anything. They then drink a mixture of boiling water that mingles with its fruit in their stomachs, and return to hell to abide in its punishment; the wording suggests that the boiling drink is outside jaḥīm itself. They earned this by finding their fathers astray and hastening to imitate them, treating their ancestors as authorities.

verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains these verses as a warning to this community’s polytheists: most earlier peoples likewise strayed, received messengers, denied them, and were destroyed, except for God’s purified, sincere servants. The oath-particles in la-qad ḍalla and la-qad arsalnā emphasize these facts; mundhirīn means the messengers, whereas mundharīn means the peoples warned.

The exception may be inclusive if Allah’s purified servants are the purified members of each nation, or exclusive if it includes the prophets as a separate group—unless prophets are included among non-prophetic servants by taghlīb. The intended meaning remains clear.

verses.75: Al-Mizan explains that the oath-particles in wa laqad nādānā and fa-la-niʿm stress God’s complete attention to Noah’s call and response. God praises Himself as the responder; the plural in al-mujībūn expresses His greatness. Noah’s call was both an imprecation against his people and a plea for divine help.
verses.76: Al-Mizan explains karb as intense sadness and understands the great calamity as either the Flood or Noah’s people’s harassment of him. Ahl includes Noah’s household and the believers associated with him, since the term can denote one’s wife and children or those connected or affiliated with him.
verses.77: Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s offspring continued to live among humankind after his time.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains taraknā as making a blessing endure, and al-ākhirīn as the peoples of later generations. As a goodly mention means that someone after a prophet upholds his mission and summons people to divine unity, perpetuating Noah’s blessing means reviving his call to divine unity and striving in God’s way, generation after generation until the Day of Resurrection.
verses.79: Al-Mizan takes al-ʿālamīn in its apparent general sense: all human peoples and nations gathered on the Day of Resurrection. Noah receives peace among them because every sound belief and good deed follows his prior example of calling to God’s oneness, refuting shirk, performing its consequent deeds, and enduring the harshest trials for almost a thousand years without associating anyone with God. He consequently shares in all good deeds until the Resurrection, and no other Qur’anic figure receives so expansive a salutation. Some instead interpret the worlds as those of angels, jinn, and humankind.
verses.80: Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s answered call, deliverance with his people, enduring progeny, and peace in all worlds were honors bestowed for his virtue. The verse likens his recompense to that of righteous people only in the general principle of good reward; it does not mean that every righteous person receives Noah’s particular reward.
verses.81: Al-Mizan explains Noah’s righteousness by his being a true faithful servant of God: he willed and acted only in accordance with God’s will, and true belief pervaded his whole existence. Nothing but beautiful goodness proceeds from such a person, which is why he was among the virtuous.
verses.82: Al-Mizan explains thumma as indicating sequence rather than a temporal interval, and al-ākhirīn as Noah’s polytheistic people.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan defines a shīʿah as those who follow another’s path step by step, whether they live before or after that person. The pronoun in min shīʿatihi refers to Noah: Abraham followed Noah in the religion of divine unity. The view that it refers to Muḥammad lacks textual evidence.

Some exegetes note a stylistic parallel in adjoining Noah’s and Abraham’s stories: Noah was a second Adam and father of humanity, while Abraham was father of the prophets, from whom the surviving religions of divine unity trace their descent. Noah was saved from drowning, and Abraham from burning.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains Abraham’s coming to his Lord as believing and having faith in Him. A sound heart contains nothing that obstructs faith or pure turning to God: no open or hidden associationism, unbecoming conduct, effects of sins, or inclination to anything besides Him. Thus it is a heart that inclines to nothing other than God. The interpretation of it as a heart free of associationism is substantially included in this meaning, whereas interpreting it as sorrowful is unsubstantiated.

The adverb idh relates to min shīʿatihi in the preceding verse; some instead connect it to an implied “remember.”
verses.85: Al-Mizan explains that Abraham asked what thing his father and people worshipped because he was astonished that they worshipped idols.
verses.86: Al-Mizan explains that Abraham asks whether they desire false, invented gods rather than God. The initial placement of if and ālihah serves emphasis.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains that Abraham asks whether they desire false, invented gods rather than God. The initial placement of if and ālihah serves emphasis.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan holds that the apparent sense links Abraham’s statement that he felt ill to his glance at the stars. He may have determined the time of a recurring illness from the stars, or his glance may have concerned the stars themselves or astrologers’ predictions. Of two views—that he foresaw the recurrence of illness, or that he read the stars as astrologers do—the first better suits Abraham’s perfect belief in divine unity, since he did not regard anything besides God as influencing events.

There is nevertheless no firm evidence that Abraham was not actually ill. Since the Qur’an says that he said he was ill and came to his Lord with a sound heart, he could not have lied or exaggerated. The most apt alternative interpretation proposed by exegetes is that he spoke evasively: perhaps he contemplated the stars as signs of God’s existence and oneness while his people mistook this for astrology, and meant only that every human being eventually falls ill. They then understood an illness to be imminent, enabling him to remain behind and break the idols. But this depends on his being healthy that day, for which there is no evidence; moreover, prophets cannot speak evasively or deceptively in a way that endangers people’s trust in them.

verses.95:
Al-Mizan explains that, after Abraham was captured and brought before the people, he rebuked them for worshipping what they themselves had hewn. God created both them and what they fashion; creation entails divine management and lordship, so it is foolish to abandon God for man-made idols. In both clauses, mā is a relative pronoun referring to the things hewn or fashioned, not a gerund-forming particle.

Calling human products part of God’s creation does not mean that God directly performs human acts. He gave people free will and does not interfere with its exercise. To say that He directly created their acts without free will would entail predestination and make the verse an excuse for idolaters rather than an argument against them.

The alternatives that it means going where God ordered or that he was dying after being cast into the fire lack evidence and conflict with the following prayer for a righteous son and the glad tidings of one.

verses.101: Al-Mizan explains that ghulām signifies a male child who would reach manhood. His forbearance, bestowed by God and expressing maturity and inward purity, later appeared when he told his father to do what he was commanded and promised patience, if Allah willed. The Qur’an calls no prophets other than this son and his father forbearing (ḥalīm).
verses.102:
Al-Mizan explains that the opening fa- passes over unmentioned events—his birth, growth, and arrival at the age of work, namely puberty. Abraham’s repeated “I see” indicates a recurring dream in which he sacrificed his son. He understood the dream as God’s command, represented by its final result, and asked his son’s view in order to test his response; fa-unẓur mādhā tarā means, “Tell me what you think,” not literal sight.

The son’s reply, “Do as you are commanded,” accepts sacrifice because it is a divine command and emphasizes that obedience is due to God’s command rather than merely saying, “Sacrifice me.” His promise of patience, qualified by “if Allah wills,” was meant to console his father against the anguish of seeing him bloodied. It also shows his refinement and recognition that patience is a gift God may grant or withhold, not a quality he independently possesses.
verses.103: Al-Mizan explains aslamā as surrendering to and being content with the divine command. Talla means to throw down, and lil-jabīn specifies that Abraham threw his son down upon one side of his forehead. The omitted result after “when” conveys the severity and bitterness of the ordeal.
verses.104:

God rewards the virtuous by testing them with trials that appear severe but are easy in reality; once they pass, He grants them the best reward in this world and the hereafter. Abraham was tested by such a clear trial.

verses.143:
Al-Mizan holds that being “among those who glorify” means that glorification had become an established and enduring quality in Jonah. Of the three views—that he glorified God before entering the whale, only while within it, or both before and within it—the first does not accord with his cry in the darkness, “There is no god but You. Glory be to You! I was wrong.” (21:87). That verse permits the second or third view, but the commentary prefers the third: the wording particularly concerns his glorification in the whale, while also indicating an established prior practice.

His confession combines God’s transcendence with his admission that he had wronged himself and felt that God had no power over him when he left his people. Thus, his glorification means that nothing deserves worship or turning to but God; God is above what Jonah’s deed might suggest, and Jonah renounces any apparent turning away from God’s service toward another. This glorification and confession were the cause of his rescue. God tested him to purify him and save him from the grief his act had brought upon himself.

The commentary understands his remaining in the fish until the day people are raised to mean that he would have remained there until the Resurrection and then been raised from it as people are raised from their graves. The verse does not establish whether he would have been alive or dead, whether the fish’s belly would have been his grave, whether the fish would have lived indefinitely, or whether “the day they are raised” denotes either blast of the trumpet or merely a very long time. Such exegetical debates therefore lack textual grounds.

verses.145: Al-Mizan explains that nabadha means to cast away, and that ʿarāʾ is a place without shade or shelter. Apparently, after Jonah became one of those who glorify God, God brought him from the fish and water onto a shadeless shore while he was ill.
verses.146: Al-Mizan explains that yaqṭīn is a squash plant with broad, round leaves, which God caused to grow so Jonah could shelter beneath it.
verses.147: Al-Mizan explains that “or more” does not express uncertainty about the number, but abundance: a hundred thousand—indeed, more. The people meant are those of Nineveh.
verses.148:
Al-Mizan explains that Jonah’s people believed him rather than calling him a liar, so God averted the approaching punishment and allowed them to live until their appointed terms. Their being granted provision or enjoyment alludes to (10:98), where their belief removes the worldly punishment of disgrace.

The commentary concludes that Jonah was sent back to the same people, not to a new community, and that after seeing punishment loom, they repented, believed, and later followed him when he returned. It rejects the view that “We sent him” (37:147) refers to a new people after his expulsion from the whale. Jonah had first called the idolatrous people of Nineveh to worship God, but left, hoping to be released from this responsibility. After the trial of the whale and his casting onto the shore, he answered God’s call, returned to summon them again, and they believed. Their respite depended on renewed belief in God’s messenger, not simply on punishment having been lifted; otherwise God would not have left them to themselves. The references to Jonah’s wrath and distress, together with (10:98), also oppose the contrary view, since punishment is called averted only when it is present or impending.

Al-Mizan says that the Qur’an relates only part of Jonah’s story. Taken together, its verses portray him as a messenger sent to more than one hundred thousand people who rejected his call until the threatened punishment approached. When they saw it, they believed and turned to God, and He removed their humiliation in this world. Jonah then learned that the punishment had been removed, apparently without knowing that they had repented; he continued onward in anger, like a slave fleeing his master and thinking his master had no power over him, and boarded a laden ship. A giant whale approached, the sailors cast lots to save the ship, and Jonah was thrown into the sea and swallowed.

God kept Jonah alive and sound in the whale for several days and nights. Recognizing the event as a divine trial over what he had done, he called out, “There is no god but You! I was wrong” (21:87). God answered, had the whale cast him upon a barren shore while he was ill, and caused a gourd-tree to grow as shelter. Once recovered, Jonah returned to his people; they answered his call, and God granted them enjoyment for a time.

The commentary notes that many Shiʿi and some Sunni narrations share elements that can be inferred from the Qur’anic verses, while differing over unmentioned details. It does not rely on disparate narrations (āḥād) to establish sacred history, since their details cannot be verified from the verses.

Al-Mizan reports that Jonah is known in Arabic as Yūnāh ibn Amtāy, and that the Old and New Testaments allude to, but do not fully recount, his story. It summarizes al-Ālūsī’s account from the People of the Book: commanded to go to corrupt Nineveh, Jonah fled toward Tarsīs; a storm endangered his ship; the lot identified him; and he was thrown overboard, swallowed by a whale, and later expelled after three days and nights of prayer. He then preached to Nineveh, whose people, king, and even animals were ordered to fast and humble themselves; their repentance led God to spare the city. In that account, Jonah was distressed that punishment had been withheld, later grieved over a gourd-tree destroyed by a worm, and was reproved for grieving over it while denying pity to Nineveh.

The commentary finds clear differences between this account and the Qur’anic one, especially its portrayal of Jonah as abandoning his prophetic office and resenting God’s mercy despite knowing that the people had repented. Although Qur’anic expressions such as his fleeing like a fugitive slave or going away in wrath may seem similar, the difference is decisive: the Biblical accounts freely attribute disobedience and even grave sins to prophets, whereas the Qur’an absolves prophets of every sin, even trivial ones. Expressions that could suggest disobedience must therefore be interpreted, in light of their context and evidence, as figurative descriptions of Jonah’s deed rather than literal abandonment of his mission.

Finally, Al-Mizan notes God’s praise of Jonah: he is among the faithful, was chosen and made among the virtuous because of his sincerity in worship, and is counted among the prophets, who surpass all other peoples in virtue and are guided to the straight path.

verses.158: Al-Mizan explains the alleged kinship as the claim that the jinn were born from God. Yet the jinn know they will be brought forth (muḥḍarūn), whether for reckoning or the Fire, and thus know that they are under God’s lordship and will be recompensed for their deeds. Their relation to God is that of servant to lord, not child to parent; a being subject to another’s lordship is not fit for worship. The view that jinnah denotes a class of angels, with “they” referring instead to the faithless, lacks Qur’anic evidence and is remote from the wording.
verses.159:
Al-Mizan initially takes yaṣifūn to refer to the previously mentioned faithless and the exception for the mukhlaṣīn as non-inclusive: God transcends either their description of Him or the things they ascribe to Him—children, kinship with creatures, and partners—while His purified, sincere servants describe Him befittingly. Interpretations that attach the exception to those “brought forth” or to those who “ascribed” kinship are unlikely.

More broadly and precisely, the verses may concern all human descriptions of God; then the exception is inclusive, because only His purified servants describe Him appropriately. Human understanding is limited, whereas God is unlimited and beyond every imagined description. God has purified servants for Himself who associate nothing with Him, know Him and all else through Him, and, when describing Him, recognize the inadequacy of speech. The Prophet, foremost among them, said: “I cannot praise you sufficiently; You are as you have praised Yourself.”

Al-Mizan treats this as a consequence of the preceding exclusion: the erroneous descriptions of God and the objects of worship cannot tempt anyone away from Him except one already following the path of the Fire; God’s purified servants do not err in describing Him. In mā taʿbudūn, mā is relative and denotes idols alone, or idols together with false gods such as demon-jinn; mā in mā antum is negative, -hi refers to God, and fātinīn means those who misguide away from Him. Other exegetes make “you and what you worship” an independent pairing and take fātinīn in the unconventional sense of imposing or burdening, so that they can impose their demigods only on those already bound for the Fire. Another possibility takes ʿalā as bi- and -hi as referring to what they worship, yielding that their worship misleads only those already on hell’s path. Al-Mizan judges these readings feigned and not required by the text.

Al-Mizan understands these as an intervening utterance of Jibraʾīl, or of Jibraʾīl with the angels who assist him in conveying revelation, like: “And we only descend at the command of your Lord; to Him belongs whatever is before us and whatever is behind us and whatever is between these. (19:64)” The alternative that the Prophet speaks for himself and the believers—each assigned a place on the Day of Judgment, arranging themselves for ritual prayer and glorifying God—is contrived and does not accord with the text.

The verses refute the self-contradictory belief that angels, though acknowledged as God’s servants under His care, independently govern their allotted parts of the cosmos. The angels deny independent will while retaining their intermediary role: “They do not precede Him in speech, and do as they are told (21:27).” Their assigned place is a specific post, not delegated free control; they are fashioned to obey, execute God’s commands, and worship Him. Their ranks are their waiting before God for commands concerning the cosmos, rather than, though possibly, ranks for prayer. Their glorification absolves God of what does not befit His majesty. Thus they receive and carry out the divine command and reject every suggestion of a partner or defect in the divine essence.

The verses refute the self-contradictory belief that angels, though acknowledged as God’s servants under His care, independently govern their allotted parts of the cosmos. The angels deny independent will while retaining their intermediary role: “They do not precede Him in speech, and do as they are told (21:27).” Their assigned place is a specific post, not delegated free control; they are fashioned to obey, execute God’s commands, and worship Him. Their ranks are their waiting before God for commands concerning the cosmos, rather than, though possibly, ranks for prayer. Their glorification absolves God of what does not befit His majesty. Thus they receive and carry out the divine command and reject every suggestion of a partner or defect in the divine essence.

verses.170: Al-Mizan explains the fa- as fāʾ faṣīḥa, implying what precedes it: the Qur’an was sent to them, but they rejected it and failed to fulfill their promise to follow a scripture. They will soon know the consequences of that rejection; this is a divine warning.
verses.171:
Al-Mizan identifies God’s word (kalimah) as His decree to aid the messengers. That it “has gone forth” (sabaqat) may mean that it was already sworn as a divine promise or already manifested by giving them power and victory; the wording, especially la-hum, makes its fulfillment certain.

Divine assistance (naṣr) is unrestricted and cannot be confined to this world, the next, or one form. It includes the proof given to messengers, since truth cannot be vanquished; help against enemies, immediately or through later divine vengeance; and aid in the hereafter. Thus, “Surely We help Our messengers, and those who believe, in this world’s life and on the day when the witnesses shall stand. (40:51)”

verses.173:
Al-Mizan explains jund as a dense assembly, hence a military contingent, close in sense to ḥizb. God’s hosts are those united in obeying the divine command and striving in His way: either the faithful alone or the prophets together with their faithful followers. Thus the faithful, like the prophets they follow, receive divine aid.

This decree of ultimate aid and victory is a social or universal law conditional upon genuine faith. Prophets and believers are God’s forces only while acting by His command and striving in His way. If they depart from faith and retain “believer” merely as a name, they cannot expect divine assistance or victory.
verses.174: Al-Mizan takes the command to turn away as consequent upon the promise of divine aid and victory, especially over the polytheists and Quraysh. “For a time” sets a near limit and therefore promises the Prophet imminent help and victory. It was fulfilled shortly thereafter through the migration to Medina and the deaths of Quraysh leaders at Badr and elsewhere.
verses.175: Al-Mizan reads the command to watch, joined to the preceding command to turn away, as indicating that the result will follow soon: the Prophet is to observe their denial and obstinacy before his warnings, while they will soon see the consequence of their denial and arrogance.
verses.176: Al-Mizan says the verse rebukes those who ask when chastisement and victory will come: they should not seek to hasten punishment. When it descends in their midst (bi-sāḥatihim), it will encompass them from every direction, and it will be a severe, fateful, and most wretched morning for those warned—the Qurayshite polytheists.

verses.178: Al-Mizan notes that exegetes commonly regard these verses as an emphatic repetition of (37:174–175). Some distinguish the first pair as earthly punishment and this pair as otherworldly punishment, but this is problematic: the earlier verse says “watch them,” whereas this says simply “watch.” The latter is therefore more general, concerning observation of how most people fall into unbelief or hypocrisy, and warns of resurrection-day torment in general.

verses.180: Al-Mizan says the verse absolves God from what the Prophet’s faithless opponents ascribed to Him. In subḥāna rabbika rabb-i al-ʿizzati, “your Lord” declares the Lord whom the Prophet worships free of their claims, while “Lord of Might” establishes that God alone possesses invincible might: none can humiliate or overpower Him or escape Him. The polytheists, enemies of truth who have been warned of punishment, can do nothing against Him.
verses.181: Al-Mizan explains this greeting of peace as encompassing all messengers and declaring their protection before God from divine torment and other miseries.
verses.182: Al-Mizan refers “praise be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds” to its exegesis of Sūrah al-Fātiḥah.
